US Stock Futures Rise as Investors Await Earnings, Central Bank Decisions and Middle East Developments: Dow Jones, S&P, Nasdaq, Wall Street
Wall Street sign in New York City ©Petr Kratochvil US stock futures moved higher on Monday as investors prepared for a week of corporate earnings announcements, central bank policy decisions and developments affecting international financial markets.
Oil prices declined following reports of diplomatic efforts to reduce tensions between the United States and Iran, while French government bonds recovered some ground after a period of political and social uncertainty.
Investors were also assessing the outcome of Brazil's presidential election, where Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva secured a fourth term following a closely contested vote.
Corporate earnings will be a major focus throughout the week, with Verizon (NYSE:VZ) among the companies scheduled to report on Monday.
US equity futures indicated a higher opening for Wall Street following declines across the three major stock indices on Friday.
At 04:43 ET (08:43 GMT), S&P 500 futures had gained 23 points, or 0.3%, while Nasdaq 100 futures were up 64 points, or 0.2%.
Dow Jones Industrial Average futures advanced 241 points, equivalent to 0.5%.
The gains followed a session in which US equities declined amid concerns about technology investment spending, interest rate expectations and geopolitical developments.
Investors have been examining the financial implications of large-scale artificial intelligence infrastructure investment, particularly the use of debt financing and the time required for projects to generate returns.
Expectations that interest rates could remain elevated for longer have also influenced equity valuations.
Meanwhile, rising oil prices and reports of possible renewed military action involving the United States and Iran contributed to market uncertainty during the previous week.
US Treasury securities attracted demand as investors assessed risks across global financial markets, although the extent to which the buying reflected a shift towards lower-risk assets remains subject to interpretation.
Oil Prices Decline Following Reports of US-Iran Diplomatic Contacts
International oil prices fell on Monday after reports that Qatari mediators had visited Tehran over the weekend to explore ways of reducing tensions between Iran and the United States.
Brent crude futures declined 1.6% to $114.92 per barrel, while US West Texas Intermediate futures fell 2.0% to $101.25 per barrel.
The declines followed a weekly increase of more than 6% in Brent crude, which recorded its highest weekly closing level since 2022.
Recent media reports suggested that US President Donald Trump was considering further military action against Iran following the November midterm elections.
Speaking to Fox News on Sunday, Trump said it was "getting to be decision time" regarding whether Washington would undertake additional strikes or pursue an agreement with Tehran.
The comments followed earlier statements about possible military operations, which prompted Iranian officials to warn of retaliatory measures.
Regional tensions have also been affected by exchanges of attacks involving Iran-backed Houthi forces in Yemen and Saudi Arabia.
These developments have raised concerns about potential disruptions to energy production and transportation in the Middle East.
The reported diplomatic contacts contributed to Monday's decline in oil prices, although no agreement resolving the tensions had been announced.
Verizon Earnings Begin a Week of US Corporate Results
Corporate earnings are expected to influence US equity trading throughout the week, with a substantial number of S&P 500 companies scheduled to release quarterly results.
Approximately one-quarter of companies in the index have reported their latest earnings so far.
According to analysts at Vital Knowledge, the results published to date indicate continued underlying demand, while cost management and price increases have contributed to company profitability.
Investors will be examining whether these trends continue across the broader market.
Technology company earnings will receive particular attention following recent concerns about spending on artificial intelligence infrastructure.
Analysts and investors are assessing whether large capital expenditure programmes and associated financing costs are affecting earnings, cash flow and future investment plans.
Verizon (NYSE:VZ) is scheduled to report before the opening of US markets on Monday.
The telecommunications company operates in a competitive environment that includes established providers AT&T and T-Mobile, as well as newer communications services associated with SpaceX.
Its results will provide updated information about operating performance and competitive conditions in the US telecommunications market.
French Bond Yields Ease After Moody's Maintains Sovereign Rating
French government bond yields edged lower on Monday as financial markets assessed developments in the country's political and fiscal situation.
The decline followed a weekend during which large-scale demonstrations appeared to subside, although labour organisations have called for further protests.
The demonstrations, initially associated with student-led action, have expanded to include concerns about wages, living costs and public services.
Labour representatives have called for additional demonstrations next weekend and a nationwide strike on 5 November.
France's financial markets also responded to a decision by Moody's on Friday to maintain the country's Aa3 sovereign credit rating.
The decision came despite expectations among some market participants that the agency might revise its assessment.
French government bond futures rose on Monday, while the euro strengthened.
The yield on France's benchmark 10-year government bond declined, indicating a recovery in bond prices.
Investors continue to monitor fiscal policy, public borrowing requirements and the potential economic effects of further industrial action.
Lula Wins Brazilian Presidential Election With 51.8% of Votes
Brazil's presidential election also attracted attention in international financial markets after Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva secured a fourth presidential term.
According to figures reported by Brazil's Superior Electoral Court, Lula received approximately 51.8% of votes, compared with 48.2% for Senator Flávio Bolsonaro, with 99% of ballots counted.
The result followed an election in which Bolsonaro had led after the first round.
Bolsonaro disputed the outcome and called for the vote to be annulled, alleging that a Supreme Court decision to extend voting hours in some areas had affected the process.
The allegations were reported as claims by Bolsonaro, rather than established findings of electoral irregularities.
Analysts at Deutsche Bank said the result differed from the outcome increasingly reflected in financial market positioning, where investors had anticipated a Bolsonaro victory.
An exchange-traded fund listed in Tokyo and tracking Brazilian equities declined during Asian trading.
Capital Economics analysts also revised their assessment of Brazil's near-term financial market outlook following the election.
In a research note, the firm said Lula's victory could affect expectations for fiscal reform and economic growth, and anticipated pressure on the Brazilian real, equities and government bonds.
These assessments represent analysts' forecasts rather than confirmed future market movements.
Investors Monitor Monetary Policy and Geopolitical Risks
The coming trading week will bring together several developments relevant to global financial markets.
US corporate earnings will provide updated information about business profitability, consumer demand and investment spending, particularly in the technology sector.
Central bank decisions will also influence expectations for borrowing costs and economic conditions.
At the same time, investors will continue to assess diplomatic developments involving the United States and Iran, the outlook for international oil supplies and political developments in France and Brazil.
Monday's gains in US equity futures and the decline in crude oil prices reflected the market movements recorded ahead of these events.

items.content:
No changes are expected in the U.S. Federal Reserve's benchmark interest rate at next week's meeting. The market takes it for granted that the U.S. monetary authority will choose to leave its monetary policy unchanged, holding rates within the 3.75%–4.00% target range set following last month's hike. According to asset management experts, the rationale is twofold: the proximity of the midterm elections and the ongoing economic resilience displayed by the United States.
"The proximity of the midterm elections, along with the need to evaluate the impact that the previous rate hike has had on the market, are among the most significant arguments for postponing a decision to raise rates again in October. Consequently, even though the September U.S. inflation print came in worse than expected across both headline and core metrics, it still appears too early to confirm an upward trend. Investors believe Warsh will opt to delay any hike until December, when the market anticipates another increase in the policy rate that will lift the target range to 4.00%–4.25%," explains Cristina Gavín Moreno, Head of Fixed Income at Ibercaja Gestión.
Furthermore, as Kish Pathak, fixed-income research analyst at MFS IM, and Erik Weisman, chief economist and portfolio manager at MFS IM, recall, comments from Vice Chairs Williams and Jefferson revealed no intention to raise rates this month. Christopher Waller stated that hikes "do not necessarily have to happen at consecutive meetings," and Bowman sees no urgency to act. Finally, Warsh's remarks in Bangkok were notable for what went unsaid: he did not repeat the forceful anti-inflation message delivered at Jackson Hole.
"Data published since the last meeting supports the view that the labor market remains in good shape and that inflation is still too elevated for comfort. At the same time, Warsh has favored focusing on broader trends. A single additional month of data does little to determine whether the trend is shifting, which is why he has advocated for reducing the number of FOMC meetings. The nature of the risks confronting the economy also counsels patience. For instance, latent inflationary pressures will ease if some resolution to the war involving Iran is reached and energy prices retreat. The economy has proven resilient amid the oil crisis thanks to robust capital expenditure linked to artificial intelligence and the wealth effect generated by equities. If the recent volatility in AI-related stocks worsens, growth could lose momentum. By December, there will be more visibility on both fronts," argue the MFS IM experts.
Bank of America (BofA) economists take a more critical view of the headline U.S. economic data, acknowledging that while there are "strong arguments for raising rates, there are substantial hurdles to executing it." They maintain their forecast that the Fed will raise interest rates by 25 basis points, although they recognize it will be a difficult decision to implement given market developments over the past week. "September inflation, coming in well above expectations, bolsters the case for an October hike. The October decision will test Fed Chair Kevin Warsh's resolve to introduce a radical shift in the institution's forward guidance. If the Fed raises rates, fears of excessive monetary tightening could emerge; if it holds rates unchanged, markets might question its credibility," they state.
Thus, according to market experts, the primary focus of next week's meeting lies in the Fed Chair's assessment of the condition of the U.S. economy. "Even if he does not deliver formal forward guidance, he can certainly offer clues about what to expect—not so much for the remainder of this year, where the market already prices in a December hike, but looking ahead to 2027. If consumer strength persists and inflationary pressures become entrenched, that could lead to two additional hikes next year," Gavín notes.
According to Christian Scherrmann, Chief U.S. Economist at DWS, in one of his rare public appearances outside the post-FOMC press conference, the Fed Chair refrained from commenting on the monetary policy outlook. "This was widely interpreted as a signal that the Fed will maintain the status quo, likely referencing his Jackson Hole remarks prior to the last rate increase. However, other Fed officials continue to send mixed signals. For example, Governor Christopher Waller still entertains the possibility of further hikes, even as higher Treasury yields tighten financial conditions. Vice Chair Philip Jefferson advocates for patience, while Governor Michelle Bowman sees little urgency to act. Others, such as Austan Goolsbee, Beth Hammack, John Williams, and Susan Collins, worry that inflation could prove stickier than expected. This divergence of views suggests the committee itself is divided over whether policy is already restrictive enough. In any case, central bankers have become more active in recent months rather than less, contrary to what Chair Warsh suggested. We interpret this as a sign of an engaged FOMC, which in our view reinforces the institution's independence," Scherrmann emphasizes.

items.content:
Image caption, Plenums are essentially closed door meetings of the Party's central committee that happen at least once a year
A major political gathering is under way in the Chinese capital, with a closed-door meeting of senior figures that could shape the look of the ruling Communist Party in the years to come.
The Fifth Plenum brings together around 300 members of the Central Committee and state media said it would pave the way for a "tightening of discipline" within the Party's ranks.
The four-day session that started on Monday will give Xi Jinping an opportunity to further consolidate his grip on power following recent purges.
The normally annual plenums are highly secretive, but a summary of decisions and a more detailed document will be made public after.
They are essentially closed door meetings of the Party's central committee that happen at least once a year.
There are usually seven plenums during each five-year Central Committee term and they are watched from afar because they are meant to signal the leadership's priorities.
The timing for this year's gathering is important because it is a year away from the next Party Congress, where a new set of priorities is set up and a new central committee appointed.
Officially, the Central Committee selects the Party's top leadership but the real processes leading to the selection are kept secret within the Party elite.
The next Party Congress will almost certainly reappoint Xi as the country's leader, following the abolition of term limits.
Past plenum sessions have been used to declare Xi as "the core" of the Party, abolish term limits which cleared the way for him to remain in power indefinitely, and elevate his personal philosophy â branded as "Xi Jinping Thought" â to the same level as Chairman Mao.
This year's plenum is an opportunity for Xi to dictate strategy in the run up to the Congress, ensuring that views are aligned and delegates loyal.
Even the location of the meeting, which will wrap up on Thursday, has not been announced. Past plenums have been held inside Beijing's Jingxi Hotel.
According to a readout from the powerful 21-member Politburo this September, the plenum will adopt a decision on "several major issues persistently advancing the comprehensive strict governance of the Party", which is being read as a way to further ensure obedience and effectiveness from distant party officials.
This means it would also be a time of nervousness for delegates as they look around the room with its "empty chairs" following the scale of recent purges within the Party.
Allegations of corruption, even "moral corruption", have seen large swathes of senior figures culled.
"Moral corruption" has been seen by experts as a way of cracking down on perceived disloyalty to Xi because overall disloyalty to the Party can be interpreted as a breach of "morality".
The Asia Society Policy Institute has estimated that of 44 military members appointed to the Central Committee in 2022 only two have not been taken down.
The all-powerful seven-man Central Military Commission, which runs the armed forces in China, has also been whittled down to only two people, Xi Jinping and one other general.
This plenum is an opportunity for him to appoint new officers to this body.

items.content:
More than three-quarters of consultants who took part in the BMA ballot voted in favour of strike action. Photograph: Jeff Moore/PA
More than three-quarters of consultants who took part in the BMA ballot voted in favour of strike action. Photograph: Jeff Moore/PA
NHS consultants to go on two-day strike in England in November
Industrial action by senior doctors to begin on 25 November with only emergency cover provided, BMA says
England’s most senior hospital doctors will strike next month in a dispute over their pay and hours, prompting NHS bosses to warn that patients will suffer “pain, discomfort and inconvenience”.
Consultant doctors, who earn an average of £152,000 a year inclusive of overtime and merit awards, will stage a two-day walkout on 25 and 26 November, as hospitals gear up for the extra pressures winter brings.
On those days, hospitals will operate with consultants providing only emergency cover, in the way they do on Christmas Day, because most will withdraw their labour.
Consultants decided to strike after 18 months of talks with the government did not lead to agreement on key issues, including their call for action to address a 25% fall in the real-terms value of their salaries since 2009-10, the British Medical Association (BMA) said. The senior doctors also want a 10% cut in their working hours.
The BMA accused ministers of ignoring consultants’ concerns about burnout related to their workloads and said last week’s well-below-inflation pay offer of a 2.4% increase for next year was the last straw.
Consultants voted in July to take industrial action. The BMA said that since then, informal talks with the Department of Health and Social Care had produced no meaningful progress, only another cut to the value of their pay.
Consultant doctors last went on strike in 2023, when they walked out for nine days. Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The Guardian Ciarán Devane, the head of the NHS Alliance, which represents NHS leaders, said he was “astonished and dismayed” by the BMA’s move at a time when the health service was working to tackle a backlog of more than 6 million patients awaiting more than 7m treatments.
“NHS leaders will be both astonished and dismayed by the BMA’s decision to proceed with walkouts by consultants at a time when plans to restore waiting time targets hang by a thread and as teams make wider preparations for winter after a gruelling summer,” Devane said. “Any decision to down tools risks throwing these plans further off course and will once again disrupt patient care while severely hitting NHS finances.
“A consultant walkout will result in non-urgent outpatient appointments, elective surgeries and follow-ups being postponed or rescheduled. While [postponement] is needed in the interests of patient safety, it will potentially leave patients in unnecessary pain, discomfort, and inconvenience.”
The BMA’s decision presents the prime minister, Andy Burnham, with a considerable challenge as he grapples with tight public finances and Labour’s aim of improving access to NHS care.
In June, resident doctors – formerly known as junior doctors – accepted a deal to end a campaign of strikes that had lasted more than three years. Consultants last staged stoppages in 2023, when they walked out for nine days during four strikes.
“Since we entered into dispute over 18 months ago we have engaged in good faith with the government, proposing practical solutions,” said Dr Helen Neary and Dr Shanu Datta, the co-chairs of the BMA’s consultants committee. “But time and time again ministers have kicked the can down the road. Unfortunately, that road has now run out, and we have been forced to announce strikes.
“Consultants take their responsibilities incredibly seriously, and striking does not come naturally, but we are hearing loud and clear from the profession that they have had enough.
“Not only is our pay still a quarter down in real terms on what it was 17 years ago, having fallen more steeply than the rest of the economy, but we are also not being given time to dedicate our all to the NHS and patients, with quality and improvement being traded for the treadmill of target-chasing, driving colleagues to burnout through excessive workloads.”
Ben Morrin, the chief executive of NHS Employers, which represents England’s 205 health trusts, urged the BMA to be realistic about what size of pay rise was affordable.
“We need to be honest and transparent about what the NHS can afford at this time. If that limit is reached and industrial action takes place, we owe it to patients to focus on delivering the safest care we can,” he said.
He added that the strike would “weaken the clinical teams in every NHS hospital, which are essential to delivering high-quality patient care this winter”.
Yvette Cooper, the health secretary, urged consultants to “not take irresponsible action that would place our health service under even greater pressure” during what would be a tough winter for the NHS.
A Department of Health and Social Care source said: “The BMA’s consultants committee is threatening strikes because they want a five-hour cut to the working week and to reduce the proportion of their week spent treating patients, changes that would cost taxpayers over £2bn. This is despite average earnings of £152,000 a year and a £25,000 increase to average earnings over the last four years.”

items.title: Warren Buffett's Favorite Stock Market Indicator Is Flashing Red. Here's What History Warns Is Coming Next. - The Motley Fool
items.summary: Warren Buffett's Favorite Stock Market Indicator Is Flashing Red. Here's What History Warns Is Coming Next.  The Motley Fool
items.content:
It's no secret the S&P 500 ( ^GSPC +0.74% ) has enjoyed an unprecedented rally in recent years, fueled mostly by enthusiasm surrounding artificial intelligence (AI) and investments in technology infrastructure. Ironically enough, it's times like these that usually have contrarian investors like Warren Buffett sitting on the sidelines instead of following the crowd.
Buffett's favorite valuation tool suggests his concerns may be justified. With stocks now trading well above levels Buffett views as extreme, history offers some important clues about what could happen next.
In an article published by Fortune in December 2001, Buffett explained how investors could assess whether the overall stock market was reasonably valued . He described the relationship between total U.S. stock market capitalization and the country's gross national product (GNP) as "probably the best single measure of where valuations stand at any given moment."
Imagine the combined market capitalization of every publicly traded American was $200 trillion while the U.S. economy produced $100 trillion in annual output. Dividing those figures generates a Buffett indicator of 200%. In other words, investors are valuing the stock market at twice the country's annual economic output.
There is one important distinction to note when calculating the Buffett indicator. Buffett originally referred to gross national product (GNP), which measures economic output attributable to U.S. residents including income earned through overseas activity. However, a more common way of calculating the Buffett indicator substitutes GNP with gross domestic product (GDP). GDP measures economic activity occurring within U.S. borders, regardless of who produces it.
According to GuruFocus, the current U.S. market-cap-to-GDP ratio hovers around 233%. Buffett says that when this indicator approaches 200% investors are "playing with fire." While the current excess in the market doesn't guarantee a crash is imminent, it does suggest investors are paying historically high prices for stocks.
History offers a stark warning when valuations become expensive
Two periods are particularly relevant today's bull market: the dot-com bubble and the market downturn between 2021 and 2022. During the late 1990s, investors were captivated by the internet. Although they were correct about the internet's revolutionary potential, many technology businesses at the time commanded unusually high valuations that proved unsustainable given the lack of revenue and profit from these companies.
Prior to the dot-com bubble bursting, the Buffett indicator peaked around 143%. Between March 2000 and October 2002, the S&P 500 declined approximately 49% while the Nasdaq Composite ( ^IXIC +1.02% ) plunged nearly 78%. What's even more devastating is that the S&P 500 did not recover its pre-dot-com high until June 2007.
Something similar happened nearly two decades later. In December 2021, the Buffett indicator was sitting just about Buffett's 200% warning sign. This was reflective of elevated stock valuations during the pandemic-era rally.
However, by mid-2022 inflation had started to surge, causing the Federal Reserve to aggressively raise interest rates. Naturally, investors began reassessing growth stocks. Between January and October 2022, the S&P 500 declined as much as 25%.
These episodes illustrate how stretched valuations often precede meaningful corrections in the market . In addition, the timing and severity of those declines are impossible to predict using the Buffett indicator in isolation.
The Buffett indicator's current reading deserves attention, but I wouldn't interpret it as absolute proof that a crash is coming.
Today's market is considerably different from the dot-com era. AI leaders such as Nvidia , Microsoft , Alphabet , Amazon , and Meta Platforms generate substantial profits because their businesses are supported by durable revenue streams rather than speculative ideas.
Meanwhile, many American companies now generate significant revenue internationally. Since the Buffett indicator compares worldwide market capitalizations with U.S. GDP, globalization can make the ratio appear higher relative to prior decades.
Nevertheless, overvalued stocks will always be vulnerable when expectations become unrealistic. If AI infrastructure spending slows, interest rates continue rising, or earnings miss expectations, investors will likely reassess the premiums they're currently paying.
This is why the smartest approach is to focus on high-quality companies with competitive advantages, strong balance sheets, consistent cash flow, and diversified business models.
Ultimately, the Buffett indicator isn't a crystal ball. But history suggests that buying stocks at historically expensive valuations will lead to disappointing returns and prolonged periods of volatility. Nevertheless, smart investors will remain invested because patience and discipline will help position your portfolio for long-term success no matter what comes next.

items.content:
The last decade has been phenomenal for investors. The S&P 500 index ( ^GSPC +0.74% ) has delivered a 322% total return (as of Oct. 23) during that time. After such a superb performance, the market has valuation concerns.
Warren Buffett first mentioned what became known as the Buffett indicator in 2001. It divides the total value of U.S. stocks by U.S. GDP (gross domestic product). A high reading might suggest that the market is overvalued relative to the economy, while a low reading can signal that it's cheap.
Currently, this metric is at 234%. That's near the highest that it's ever been.
So, is the Buffett indicator flashing a clear warning sign to investors? Here's what you need to know about the stock market right now.
The initial reaction from investors is that the stock market is currently extremely overvalued. The benchmark index has climbed at an annualized pace of roughly 15% in the past 10 years. This is much higher than its historical yearly average of 10%.
Besides the Buffett indicator, which obviously gets a lot of attention because of who it's named after, the cyclically adjusted price-to-earnings (CAPE) ratio , now at 40.6, is also at extreme levels. It was only higher during the dot-com bubble period at the turn of the 21st century. At that time, the Buffett indicator was around 135%. That's considerably lower than where it currently sits.
The 2000s were a disappointing decade for stocks, though there was a severe housing-led recession toward the end of the decade. It's also worth highlighting Warren Buffett's interpretation. A reading above 120% could be considered expensive. This means that the next 10 years may yield very poor returns.
Understanding this backdrop, it's easy to understand why investors might adopt a cautious view. A bear market, defined as a drop of at least 20% from a recent high, could always be on the horizon. And there's a possibility that the economy slips into a recession.
Plus, it's impossible to ignore how important artificial intelligence (AI) has become. If the spending boom shows any signs of slowing, it could trigger a bear market and a recession.
The smartest investors take the time to understand the current environment. However, they also know that this time is different. The Buffett indicator has shortcomings. Therefore, I don't believe it's a warning sign.
This figure fails to account for overseas revenue generated by companies. The economy has only become more global and interconnected. And many of the largest businesses in the U.S. have substantial operations in foreign markets.
This is especially true for major technology enterprises. They generate a lot of sales outside the U.S. This isn't reflected in the GDP figure, which is the denominator of the Buffett indicator. And given their massive scale, they account for a sizable share of the stock market, as reflected in the numerator. That creates an imbalance.
There's also significantly more liquidity in the economy and financial system. The M2 money supply has expanded rapidly in the last two decades, going from $6.9 trillion to $23.3 trillion today. This is due to the Federal Reserve's monetary policy decisions. There's no doubt that some of this capital has flowed to equities, adding buying pressure to stocks and lifting valuations.
Informed investors should be aware of the Buffett indicator. However, they shouldn't use it as a predictive tool to time the market. Trying to avoid downturns usually backfires, as it's virtually impossible to successfully trade in and out of positions on the right days.
Historically, the S&P 500 index has posted positive gains over every rolling 20-year period. That's really the only data point to focus on. Optimism and patience are rewarded in the stock market.

Could a tough stance toward China solve Europeâs own problems? - Global Times
Could a tough stance toward China solve Europeâs own problems?
By Xiong Rui and Wang Shuo Published: Oct 26, 2026 08:42 PM
Recently, as the EU contemplates expanding restrictions on Chinese imports, "Europe getting tough on China" has become a headline pushed by several Western media outlets, with some even urging Washington to follow Europe's steps.
For Europe, a tough stance toward China reflects a deep-seated anxiety over its shifting relative strength and growing worries about its domestic and international environment.
Currently, Europe is locked in structural economic headwinds. Although its economy gradually recovered following the sovereign debt crisis, deep-rooted issues like a lack of growth momentum have proven difficult to resolve. High energy costs, underinvestment and market fragmentation remain intertwined.
As Chinese firms gain ground in Europe's traditional strongholds and the US leverages policies to draw global capital, Europe finds itself caught in a double squeeze: terrified of its domestic industries losing their competitive edge, while fearful of capital, factories and jobs fleeing overseas at the same time.
Solving these structural dilemmas demands sustained investment, the dismantling of entrenched interest barriers and the delicate reconciliation of internal divisions. By contrast, scapegoating its troubles on a "China shock" requires far less political capital than pushing through painful domestic reforms. This largely explains why some European figures are so eager to point the finger at competitors for "not playing by the rules," while failing to reflect on their own problems.
Europe faces the dual pressure of status anxiety and security reliance. Certain European leaders worry that a relative decline in economic clout will render Europe increasingly powerless in major-power geopolitical competition.
In the calculations of some European strategists, taking a hard line on China appears to offer a catch-all solution: Domestically, framing it as safeguarding economic security addresses protectionist calls and secures support from voters and special interest groups; externally, aligning on China policy creates common ground with Washington, demonstrating to the US that Europe still holds strategic value in exchange for security guarantees.
Yet, the fatal flaw in this strategy is that a temporary alignment between Washington and Brussels on Beijing cannot paper over their divergences regarding tariffs, industrial policy and defense burden-sharing. Even if their direction of "de-risking" from China aligns on paper, endless disputes remain over who builds new capacity, who captures market share and who sets the global rules.
Furthermore, Washington has its own geopolitical calculus when managing ties with Beijing. While Europe escalates its pressure on China, the US quietly retains room for engagement and deal-making. If Europe blindly sacrifices its cooperation with China merely to prove its loyalty, it is unlikely to secure the firm security commitments it craves in return.
Taking a tough stance on China will not solve Europe's problems; it risks creating far more. Evading domestic reform by building external walls will fail to remedy Europe's competitiveness deficit. Squeezing the space for cooperation with China risks depriving European businesses of crucial market access and supply chain synergies, while piling on higher production costs and green transition burdens.
The starting point for Europe's China policy ought to be firmly grounded in its own long-term interests. While protecting industrial interests is entirely legitimate, trade protectionism must be rooted in facts and international rules. Fair market competition never guarantees that any single player will win forever.
Europe's own history demonstrates that enduring peace cannot exist without mutual respect for interests, nor without dedicated efforts to translate shared interests into reality. This historic lesson should not be tossed aside when China is involved, nor should the vast common interests between Beijing and Brussels be selectively ignored in a bid to pander to Washington. For the transatlantic relationship, casting China as a common adversary may buy a fleeting moment of alignment, but it will never foster true, long-term cohesion.
If Europe wishes to command respect and achieve genuine strategic autonomy, it must rely on its own concrete actions.

items.title: Who should win the men's Ballon d'Or? BBC Sport pundits have their say
items.summary: The Ballon d'Or winner will be announced in London on Monday - but who is going to claim the showpiece award?
items.content:
Image caption, Who should win the men's Ballon d'Or?
The Ballon d'Or winner will be announced in London on 26 October - but who is going to win it?
Bookmakers have Spain winger Lamine Yamal and England captain Harry Kane very close together as clear favourites.
Lamine Yamal won La Liga with Barcelona and the World Cup with Spain, while Kane scored 73 goals for German champions Bayern Munich and England.
Eight-time winner Lionel Messi, of Argentina and Inter Miami, and Real Madrid's France forward Kylian Mbappe are the other probable candidates.
Or how about one of Paris St-Germain's back-to-back European champions?
BBC Sport asked several of its football experts who they think should take home the award.
Figure caption, Our pundits pick their men's Ballon d'Or winner
Goal, assist... goal-kick - Kane underlines Ballon d'Or credentials
Lamine Yamal 'completes football' at 19 as Argentina betray Messi
How PSG's Ballon d'Or duo are pushing each other on
Image caption, Lamine Yamal is just one of five teenagers to start a World Cup final and win it
European football expert Guillem Balague: Can you imagine this Ballon d'Or not won by a PSG player or a Spanish player? Impossible. So gone is Kylian Mbappe.
The PSG players, there are so many of them that deserve it - Fabian Ruiz, Khvicha Kvaratskhelia, Ousmane Dembele, Vitinha. So the vote is going to be split.
There is only one Spaniard who deserves it, and that's Lamine Yamal, who has given us individual performances, collective trophies, and has that aura. He's going to win it.
Image caption, Khvicha Kvaratskhelia is a two-time Champions League winner with PSG
European football expert Julien Laurens: I think he was the best player in Europe last season, especially in the Champions League where he was outstanding. He helped lead the team to another title, a back-to-back one.
He got the penalty in the final, scored in both semi-finals, in the quarter-final, and in the last 16. He was amazing in those huge, huge games where you want your best players to step up. He deserves to win the Ballon d'Or for being the best player in the world all the way up to the World Cup.
He won't win it, unfortunately, because Lamine Yamal, for the player he is and how entertaining and spectacular he is, didn't really shine at the World Cup, even if Spain won it. He didn't really do that well in the Champions League for Barcelona, getting knocked out early. However, his style of football means he'll probably win it - but it should be Kvaratskhelia.
Ex-Liverpool and Blackburn full-back Stephen Warnock : I think it will be Lamine Yamal for helping Spain to win the World Cup. If you were asking who else is in the hunt, I would say Michael Olise, but my pick personally would be Khvicha Kvaratskhelia, he is unbelievable. I love watching him play. He had such an impact for Paris St-Germain and last season he was incredible. I just don't think he will get the votes with Georgia not being in the World Cup.
BBC Radio 5 Live Euro Leagues guest and Athletic reporter Rory Smith: It will probably go to Lamine Yamal because it generally goes to someone who has won the biggest trophy, and this is the World Cup. It shouldn't be him because he wasn't necessarily Spain's most important player but his fame and talent means it will be him.
Personally I would give it to Kvaratskhelia. He has been the most exciting player in European club football for a while now, a valuable part of the PSG team who retained the Champions League, and crucially I think you shouldn't suffer because you come from a country who isn't in the running to win the World Cup.
Image caption, Harry Kane scored six goals at the 2026 World Cup for England
Former England striker Alan Shearer: The winner of the Ballon d'Or should be Harry Kane. His numbers for the last 12 to 18 months have been absolutely sensational for Bayern and for England. For that reason, he should get it.
Ex-England midfielder Danny Murphy: My choice for the Ballon d'Or is Harry Kane. I think his goalscoring has been relentless, brilliant. He's had one of the best seasons of his career and it'll be a great reward for him if he gets the trophy. He's been brilliant at Bayern Munich since he's been there, adapted really well and he's been the best centre-forward in the world for the last 12 months.
Former Tottenham and Crystal Palace forward Andros Townsend : Harry Kane should win the Ballon d'Or. He scored 73 goals in 65 games, 36 of those in the Bundesliga. He led Bayern Munich to the league and cup double. He scored 14 goals in the Champions League, helping Bayern Munich to the semi-finals and scored six goals in the World Cup, leading England to the semi-finals. He has had an outstanding year.
Figure caption, Why Kane deserves to win the Ballon d'Or
Former England striker Ellen White : It's a tough one but I'll go with my heart - I'd love to see Harry Kane win it. I know he didn't win the World Cup but his numbers are absolutely extraordinary, with what he has achieved with Bayern Munich and England. Lamine Yamal had a few injuries but I know he won the World Cup and I'm sure he will win the Ballon d'Or one day. Michael Olise has also been phenomenal.
Norwegian football journalist Lars Sivertsen on Champions League Match of the Day: I would like to see Harry Kane win it, he deserves it. He is a real leader at Bayern Munich. He never makes trouble and is a role model. But I do wonder if him being a low-key character hurts him. The Ballon d'Or is a popularity contest. I love that he doesn't do all that but maybe he should.

The Morning Bull - US Market Morning Update Monday, Oct, 26 2026
US stocks are set for a cautiously positive open, with sentiment driven less by overseas moves and more by a single question: Can the Federal Reserve ignore stubborn inflation expectations when growth data still look strong?
The University of Michigan survey pegs year-ahead inflation expectations at 4.7% in October 2026, a five-month high. At the same time, the US Composite PMI sits at 57.6, pointing to firm business activity and resilient demand.
That mix of sticky inflation views and solid output keeps pressure on borrowing costs. Higher expected policy rates can filter into corporate funding costs, squeeze interest-sensitive business models, and narrow the cushion in earnings estimates if pricing power weakens.
The unresolved issue is how the Fed weighs that 4.7% inflation outlook against strong PMIs when it meets next week. Either growth or prices will need to blink first, and current positioning in US equities reflects that policy fork in the road.
Microsoft heads into a busy earnings week under a spotlight, as traders question when heavy AI spending will feed through to profits. items.title: Mortgage rates above 7% are the 'new normal'—here's why
items.summary: High inflation and competition for investor dollars are helping keep longer-term interest rates elevated, economists say.
items.content:
Mortgage rates above 7% are the 'new normal'—here's why
Spend Waiting for homebuying to get more   affordable? Don't hold your breath
Spend The 10 most in-demand ZIP   codes for homebuyers in 2026
Save and Invest What higher for longer interest   rates mean for your investments
Work His gas station speakeasy brought in about $5 million in one year:   Behind the hidden door, it's still the 'roaring twenties'
Spend Homes are selling below asking in 38   of the 50 biggest U.S. cities
Everyone seems to agree that mortgage rates above 7% are the new "normal."
The phrase keeps popping up lately in public comments from housing economists, including Lawrence Yun , chief economist for the National Association of Realtors, and Robert Dietz , chief economist for the National Association of Home Builders.
It's a sentiment increasingly reflected in forecasts, too, with major housing groups predicting mortgage rates will remain above 7% well into 2027. Fannie Mae forecasts mortgage rates could average 7.5% in 2027, while the Mortgage Bankers Association expects them to remain above 7% .
That means the 3% or 4% mortgage rates borrowers were used to in the years before 2022 are unlikely to return anytime soon.
"We could definitely see some movement up and down depending on data, but we're just not in the same economic environment we were in during the 2010s or the pandemic," says Jenna Stauffer, a broker and market analyst with Sotheby's International Realty.
Mortgage rates tend to move with the 10-year Treasury yield, which serves as a benchmark because mortgages are typically paid off or refinanced well before their 30-year term. And there are reasons to think those longer-term borrowing costs could remain elevated.
One is persistently high inflation. When inflation remains elevated, investors generally demand higher yields on long-term bonds to compensate for the declining purchasing power of the money they'll eventually be repaid. Inflation, as measured by the Fed's preferred PCE price index, hasn't been below the central bank's 2% target since February 2021 .
But inflation isn't the only factor. The federal government is borrowing heavily , while the artificial intelligence boom is fueling enormous private investment in data centers, power generation and other infrastructure, says Selma Hepp, chief economist at real estate data firm Cotality. Together, that increased demand for capital can put upward pressure on longer-term borrowing costs, she says.
Compared to the 2010s, "we've moved from a world with more capital than investment opportunities to one with tremendous competition for capital," Hepp says. Low inflation, abundant savings and relatively weak demand for capital helped keep mortgage rates low during that period, she says.
Demand for mortgage bonds has weakened, too , putting upward pressure on mortgage rates. Banks have become more reluctant to hold mortgage-backed securities since the 2022-23 rate spike produced steep losses on bond portfolios, says Tom Graff, chief investment officer at wealth management firm Facet. That's because bond prices generally fall when interest rates rise. The failures of Silicon Valley Bank and First Republic also prompted greater regulatory scrutiny of banks' bond holdings, he says.
During the pandemic, the Fed pushed rates in the opposite direction. The Federal Reserve bought large quantities of Treasury bonds and mortgage-backed securities to push longer-term borrowing costs lower, helping drive mortgage rates to historic lows. The Fed has since stepped away from actively buying mortgage-backed securities, says Steve Kaminski, head of residential lending at TD Bank.
With those low-rate conditions no longer in place, "mortgage rates will likely remain elevated for at least the next year," Kaminski says.
Getting mortgage rates back to around 6% would likely require lower inflation, slower economic growth or less pressure from government borrowing to help bring down the 10-year Treasury yield, Hepp says.
Kaminski similarly says getting below 7% would require lower inflation and lower Treasury yields. A weakening economy could also push rates lower as investors seek the relative safety of Treasury bonds, lowering their yields, he says.
Whether that happens is uncertain, which is why Hepp says she doesn't like calling 7% the "new normal," since there's nothing permanent about that particular number. But the low inflation, abundant capital and accommodative Fed policies that helped produce 3% and 4% mortgages are no longer in place, she says.
For would-be homebuyers, that means waiting for significantly lower mortgage rates could be a gamble.
"I don't think we should expect to return to the financial conditions that routinely produced 3% and 4% mortgages," Hepp says.
